title: ShadowBench: Exposing Lexical Anchoring and the Illusion of Forgetting in Large Language Models
Is Your Robot's Memory Just a Clock? Temporal Shortcuts in Memory-Augmented VLA Policies
Levodopa boosts hippocampal activity and strengthens generalizable rule representations in prefrontal cortex during the inference of meaning
abstract: Dopamine has long been implicated in a variety of higher-order cognitive functions, including language processing. However, the neural processes and representations by which dopamine influences language processing remain unclear. Here we show that administration of levodopa to young healthy volunteers (n = 70, 47 females) boosts hippocampal processing and neural representations of generalizable abstract rules for successful inference of novel word meaning. We used a novel experimental paradigm that required participants to build new artificial word meanings by inferring and applying abstract affixation rules. A repetition suppression procedure was combined with multivariate representational similarity analyses to isolate the neural locus of both the abstract rules required for the compositional inference process, as well as the novel word meaning representations that were composed based on these abstract rules. Levodopa modulated not only inference-related signals in the hippocampal formation, but also abstract rule representations in the medial frontal cortex. These results support the hypothesis that dopamine boosts hippocampal activity and strengthens prefrontal representations of abstract rules when building novel meaning. Significance statement Dopamine has long been implicated in a variety of higher-order cognitive functions, including language processing. However, the neural processes by which dopamine boosts language processing have remained unclear. Here we show that administration of levodopa to young healthy volunteers enhances hippocampal activity and strengthens prefrontal representations of generalizable abstract rules when building novel word meanings.

title: Hippocampal somatostatin neurons gate context generalization during fear memory updating
abstract: Abstract Freezing is used as a readout of fear memory in rodents, but it remains unclear how distinct freezing features reflect discrimination and generalization of threatening and neutral contexts. Using pose-tracking and unsupervised analysis in male and female mice undergoing contextual fear conditioning, we show that fear in neutral a context is expressed through fragmented freezing that resist experience-dependent updating, in contrast with more sustained, uninterrupted, and adaptable freezing in a threatening context. Neuronal recordings revealed that recalling neutral context fear is associated with increased activity of dentate gyrus somatostatin inhibitory neurons (SST INs). Chemogenetic suppression of SST INs during fear memory updating selectively facilitated neutral context freezing adaptation while activation prevented generalization of contextual information by restricting long-term fear reduction in contexts that differed from the updating context. These findings identify DG SST INs as context-specific modulators of fear memory updating and suggest that freezing dynamics serve as a behavioral signature of generalization.

title: GABAergic inhibition of the nucleus reuniens stabilizes post-learning quiet states and enhances memory consolidation.
abstract: Quiet states provide a permissive context for processes that benefit from reduced engagement with the environment, such as memory consolidation, but the circuit mechanisms that stabilize these states remain unclear. The midline thalamic nucleus reuniens (RE) regulates hippocampal-cortical interactions during memory consolidation, but its role in stabilizing post-learning quiet states is unknown. Here, we tested the effects of RE inhibition on quiet-state stability and memory consolidation in freely behaving rats. Following object-place recognition training, rats received RE microinfusions of muscimol or vehicle and we monitored their behavior during the subsequent period. We found that RE inhibition increased the duration of quiet bouts and reduced bout fragmentation. Twenty-four hours later, muscimol-treated rats showed enhanced object-place recognition memory. These findings suggest that RE regulates the stability of quiet states that facilitate memory consolidation and provide a circuit mechanism linking thalamic inhibition, quiet states, and memory function.

title: Sensory cortical disinhibition underlies long-term fear memory in humans
abstract: Abstract How transient threats turn into persistent, long-term fear memories is a fundamental problem in neuroscience, yet the underlying mechanisms remain elusive. Early sensory cortex, traditionally viewed as a passive feature analyzer, is increasingly recognized as an active participant in fear processing. Combining high-definition α-frequency transcranial alternating current stimulation (HD α-tACS) with simultaneous EEG-fMRI (electroencephalography-functional magnetic resonance imaging) and transformer-based neural decoding, we tracked fear memory development across formation, consolidation, and long-term retention (assessed at 15 min, 24 h, and 7 days after fear conditioning). Spatiotemporal memory traces were identified at all three assessments, beginning at an early sensory stage (40–60 ms post-stimulus) and distributed across visual cortex and limbic regions. Conditioning potentiated occipital α-oscillation desynchronization, a marker of visual cortical disinhibition, which subsequently predicted the strength of long-term memory traces. Critically, targeted α-tACS over early visual cortex induced early visual cortical (V1/V2) inhibition, abolished conditioning-potentiated α desynchronization, and selectively disrupted fear-memory consolidation and retention while leaving initial acquisition intact. These findings establish sensory cortical disinhibition as a necessary mechanism for long-term fear memory in humans and identify early sensory cortex as crucial node for intervention of persistent maladaptive fear.

title: Traveling back and forth through time: oscillatory brain patterns distinguish directional cued recall
abstract: It is well established that episodic memory involves forming associations among stimuli within an event and between the event and its spatial and temporal context and that those associations can subsequently guide the strategies and search processes that lead to successful retrieval. While countless studies have characterized the neurocognitive correlates of relational memory, how retrieval precisely relies on the associations formed between consecutive events, as well as their correspondence with a representation of past time, is less understood. The current study sought to test how transitions are made across memories according to time by directly contrasting, behaviorally and neurally, retrieval in the forward versus backward directions. A list-learning paradigm was employed with immediate cued recall tasks in which subjects had to use cue words to recall those that came next (forward) or previously (backward) in the list. Scalp EEG data acquired just before the recalled words had to be reported was then used, in combination with multivariate pattern-classification analysis (MVPA), to distinguish neural activity related to retrieval deliberation and search processes. The main results provide novel evidence that, even while equating behavioral performance across retrieval direction, high-frequency (gamma-band) oscillatory EEG activity distinguishes forward and backward retrieval. Implications of the findings are discussed in relation to other, widely-used experimental and neuropsychological tasks (e.g., serial and free recall), as well as to work on understanding the broader role of time (i.e., past versus future) in episodic memory.

title: Probing spatiotemporal context reveals differences between true and false memories.
abstract: Our memories do not faithfully represent the past, but rather are reconstructive, rendering them susceptible to the intrusion of false memories. However, the nature of the false memories is debated: Do false memories reflect the retrieval of a genuine, erroneous memory trace, or are they the product of semantic associations? This question reflects the fact that although some findings suggest that false memories can be phenomenologically compelling and rich in details, others suggest that there are subtle cues that distinguish true and false memories. Here, we take a novel approach to this question by assessing memory for the spatiotemporal context of false memories - the when and where of those memories. We demonstrate that context memory can provide a probabilistic cue to whether a memory is true or false in the Deese-Roediger-McDermott paradigm. Across participants, the reliability of reported context memory (i.e., the consistency with which people report remembering when or where a false memory occurred) revealed differences between true and false memories. Additionally, confidence in memory for context (both within and across participants) differed between true and false memories - even when controlling for confidence in having encountered the false memory. However, these effects were malleable: Under certain circumstances, false memories appeared to have genuine context traces. Together, these data provide new insights into the circumstances under which true and false memories differ in subtle but meaningful ways, speaking to theories of how false memories may arise from the reconstructive nature of memory.

title: Retrosplenial cortex exhibits parallel directional codes and contributes to medial entorhinal spatial coding in 3D curved-surface navigation.
abstract: Spatial coding is well studied in 2D, but directional and positional coding across 3D curved surfaces remains unclear. Two-photon calcium imaging in freely moving mice in a cylindrical arena indicates two directional representations in the retrosplenial cortex (RSC). In one, preferred directions shift systematically around the sidewall yet remain coherent with top-platform tuning; this organization persists in darkness with reduced precision. In the other, preferred directions remain stable across sidewall positions and are largely preserved in darkness. Medial entorhinal cortex (MEC) contains fewer, less stable direction-tuned neurons than RSC but shows more precise positional coding. MEC-projecting RSC neurons carry more precise directional and positional information than the RSC population. RSC inhibition selectively degrades MEC sidewall positional precision and cross-cylinder angular alignment in darkness. These findings indicate parallel RSC directional representations and suggest intact RSC activity contributes to stable MEC positional coding during 3D curved-surface navigation, particularly with limited visual support.

title: Information formatting in neuronal populations predicts differential functional contributions to behavior
abstract: Neurons throughout the brain encode essentially everything, so why have distinct areas? We proposed that areas format different information sources differently, implying their computational role. Here we compared the middle temporal (MT) area, involved in visual motion perception, and the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC), implicated in decision-making and reward. In a task that required monkeys to combine motion and reward information, both regions encoded both motion and reward, but formatted differently. Area MT represented them separably, whereas the dlPFC combined them in a decision-related format. A recurrent network model trained to reproduce that formatting predicted a distinct effect of stimulating those areas. Consistent with predictions, MT stimulation biased choices whereas dlPFC stimulation produced 'winner-take-all' outcomes. Our findings suggest that a modular structure flexibly reformats information to enable complex behaviors.

code_avail_evidence: Code for analysis and training of the RNN model is available via GitHub at https://github.com/solkm/formattingRNN.

title: Symmetry as a common origin of hierarchical emergence and abstraction.
abstract: Many systems of interest exhibit nested emergent layers with their own rules and regularities, and our knowledge about them seems naturally organized around these levels. How do such hierarchical structures arise, and why should observers track these hierarchies so closely? This paper proposes symmetry as an answer to both questions. By combining principles from information theory, group theory, and statistical mechanics, it is shown that dynamical processes that are equivariant with respect to a symmetry group give rise to multiple emergent macroscopic levels arranged according to the algebraic structure of the symmetry. The same symmetries shape the Bayesian beliefs of an observer with only partial access to the system, yielding a matching hierarchy of "abstract" beliefs that can be updated autonomously at different levels of resolution. These ideas are illustrated in Hopfield networks, where familiar macroscopic quantities emerge from known symmetries, and in Boolean models of gene regulation, where symmetries are instead found from the dynamics. The computational advantages provided by symmetry are showcased in Ehrenfest diffusion and epidemic modeling, where abstract beliefs enable Bayesian inference over exponentially large state spaces. These results identify symmetry as a sufficient mechanism for hierarchical emergence and-at the same time-for the capacity of abstract beliefs to mirror the systems they track, making feasible inferential problems that would otherwise be intractable.

title: A Variational Principle for the Emergence of Neural Geometry Underlying Bayesian-Like Behavior
abstract: Neural population geometry constrains how task variables are represented and read out into behavior. We propose a variational principle in which learning balances task accuracy and representational smoothness under stimulus-dependent weighting. This balance links stimulus statistics to the shape of a latent neural coordinate. For magnitude estimation, the principle predicts distortions near the edges of bounded ensembles, global affine contraction for Gaussian ensembles, and warping toward high-probability regions for bimodal ensembles. We test the bounded-uniform case in recurrent neural networks trained to reproduce time intervals. Their learned geometries occupy three regimes as the boundary distortions change from too narrow to resolve, to measurable, to extending across the stimulus range. A shape parameter selected from an empirical neural coordinate predicts the nonlinear component of mean behavior through an affine readout, with only behavioral gain and offset fitted afterward. In this bounded-uniform setting, the variational coordinate and Bayesian least-squares mean response have closely matching shapes after affine normalization. These results suggest a variational account of how stimulus statistics shape neural geometry and yield Bayesian-like behavior.

title: The Noncanonical Hippocampus: Shared and Distinct Features of the CA2FCIG Hippocampal System
abstract: The hippocampal CA2 region has received considerable interest in recent decades, earning a functional understanding beyond the previously held view as a small transitional zone. However, related hippocampal structures called the fasciola cinereum (FC) and indusium griseum (IG) have been largely neglected to date. While CA2, FC, and IG are typically presented as discontinuous structures on conventional atlases, recent work unveils a surprisingly high degree of overlapping gene expression and anatomical continuity, raising questions of their shared versus distinct functions. Here we review the molecular, anatomical, physiological, and behavioral features of each area, to begin to address whether these regions are subcomponents of a greater hippocampal structure or independent entities with distinct contributions to physiology and disease. Early evidence supports that the CA2FCIG axis is indeed a cohesive network unified by shared molecular and anatomical profiles, although regional differences in structure and function need to be taken into account. Notably, transcriptomics has revealed multiple subclusters within this complex of structures with no region-specific cell types, raising the need to understand whether cell types or anatomical subfields are the main functional units of this system. This conceptualization of these noncanonical hippocampal areas as a unified, multifaceted system raises many questions discussed here, along with the need for coordinated investigation across regions in future work.
